author: John Chrysostom
addressee: a congregation celebrating the feast of the martyr Romanus
occasion: A festal homily delivered on the commemoration of the martyr Romanus, who was executed by having his tongue cut out during a persecution.
argument: Chrysostom opens by celebrating the martyrs as members of one body with the Church, using the image of martyrs as the head and Christians as the feet, so their victory is a shared joy. He then praises love as greater even than martyrdom and asks why the devil had Romanus's tongue cut out rather than killing him outright. He explains that Romanus had been strengthening wavering Christians, so the devil hoped to silence his encouragement and make him watch helplessly as his fellow Christians fell. God overturned this scheme: after the tongue was removed, Romanus continued to speak by divine grace, with a spiritual voice greater than nature, so that angels and humans gathered to hear. Chrysostom presents this as a proof of God's power and a foreshadowing of the resurrection, comparing it to Aaron's rod that blossomed because the priesthood was dishonored, while Romanus's mouth blossomed because Christ the great high priest was blasphemed. He closes by urging the congregation to imitate Romanus's endurance and trust God's help.

outline.move: Chrysostom introduces the feast and explains why the Church rejoices in the martyrs' victories as its own members, using the body metaphor and urging the congregation to learn to rejoice with those who succeed.
He praises love as greater even than martyrdom, introduces the persecution context, and begins to examine why the devil attacked Romanus's tongue.
He describes the persecution and how Romanus strengthened and emboldened his fellow Christians, provoking the devil's focused attack, and presents the devil's imagined reasoning.

He explains the devil's cunning in cutting out the tongue rather than the head, and how God turned the scheme upside down by enabling Romanus to speak without it, with a spiritual voice that drew angels and humans.

He argues that even if Romanus had become mute, the tongue's removal would itself prove the devil's defeat, uses musical instrument analogies, and presents the voice without a tongue as a sign of resurrection, quoting David.
He compares the miracle to Aaron's rod that blossomed, then closes with exhortation, thanksgiving, and a doxology.

cast.name: Romanus
cast.who: The martyr commemorated in the homily, whose tongue was cut out during persecution.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, quoted repeatedly on love, sympathy, and spiritual warfare.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: Mentioned as one whom Herod beheaded, contrasted with Romanus.

cast.name: Herod
cast.who: The ruler who beheaded John the Baptist, contrasted with the devil's treatment of Romanus.

cast.name: Aaron
cast.who: The Old Testament priest whose rod miraculously blossomed, cited as a parallel to Romanus's mouth.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The psalmist, quoted on God's wonderful name and praise from infants' mouths.

voices.speaker: the devil (imagined)
voices.how_marked: introduced by φησίν or similar verbs of saying, presenting his internal reasoning

voices.how_marked: introduced by λέγων, φησίν, or γράφων

key_terms.sense: A Christian who bore witness to Christ by suffering or death
The act or state of bearing witness to Christ through suffering
Love, especially the love that binds Christians together and to Christ
The tongue, the physical organ of speech cut out from Romanus
The voice or speech that continued miraculously after the tongue was removed
The devil, the enemy who schemes against Christians
The crown or wreath of victory awarded to martyrs
Resurrection, especially of bodies, foreshadowed by the voice surviving the tongue's removal
Confession of faith in Christ, the act for which martyrs suffer
Divine grace or favor, the power enabling the martyr's miraculous speech
The Church, the body of believers who share in the martyrs' glory

scripture: The author quotes the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering and cites Paul's epistles by addressee (e.g., 'to the Corinthians'). Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, for Psalms, the Hebrew numbering where it differs from the Septuagint.
uncertain: The exact date of Romanus's martyrdom and the specific persecution under which he died.
The precise identity of the persecuting rulers described in section 2.
Whether the homily was delivered in Antioch or Constantinople.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Romanus continued to speak by divine grace, with a spiritual voice greater than nature, so that angels and humans gathered to hear
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἐξεκόπτετο γλῶττα, ἡ δὲ τῆς χάριτος ἐφίπτατο τῷ στόματι τοῦ μακαρίου... καὶ πάντες συνέτρεχον, ἄνωθεν ἄγγελοι, κάτωθεν ἄνθρωποι, ἕκαστος χωρὶς γλώττης στόμα ἰδεῖν ἐπιθυμοῦντες, καὶ ἀκοῦσαι φθεγγομένου οὕτως
_unresolved_facts.fix: Romanus's mouth was granted a spiritual voice by divine grace, and angels and humans gathered to see a mouth without a tongue and to hear one speaking thus—the text emphasizes the wonder of the spectacle (ἰδεῖν) as much as hearing

_unresolved_facts.fix: He praises Romanus specifically for showing great love together with martyrdom, introduces the persecution context, and begins to examine why the devil attacked Romanus's tongue
